mainTopic: The injurer's payments: sources for paying צער and ריפוי along with נזק, cases of each payment without נזק, how שבת is measured, and רבא's and רבה's questions about combined and temporary injuries.
overview: This amud covers what a person who injures someone must pay. First the גמרא finishes showing that the extra wording 'פצע תחת פצע' teaches two things: an injurer is liable even בשוגג or באונס, and he pays צער along with נזק. Next, רב פפא in the name of רבא learns from 'ורפא ירפא' that ריפוי is also paid along with נזק. The גמרא defends this against two challenges by pointing to the exact wording of the פסוק. It then gives examples where צער, ריפוי, שבת and בושת are each owed with no נזק at all. A ברייתא explains why measuring שבת as a 'watchman of cucumbers' is fair: the better jobs were already paid for in the value of the limb. רבא matches each injury to the job the victim can still do, and says that deafness requires paying the victim's whole value. רבא then asks whether separate injuries that end in deafness are paid one by one, and the question ends in תיקו. Finally רבה asks about a weakened hand that will heal, and a proof from a משנה begins that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The verse is needed to include unintentional and forced injury
steps.stepSummary: The challenge ends: 'פצע תחת פצע' is needed to teach that someone who injures by accident or under force is liable, just like someone who injures on purpose.
steps.simpleTranslation: [This verse is needed] to include someone who injures by accident, just like someone who injures on purpose, and someone forced by circumstances, just like someone who acts willingly!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a challenge from the line before this section. It says the phrase 'פצע תחת פצע' is already used for a different lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא learned from 'פצע תחת פצע' that one pays צער along with נזק. The challenge here says the phrase is needed to make the injurer liable even when he acted בשוגג or באונס. If so, it may not be free to teach about צער.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who acts by accident, without meaning to
Someone forced by circumstances beyond his control
To include (extra cases in a law)

phrases.english: To include one who acts by accident like one who acts on purpose
phrases.notes: The פסוק here is 'פצע תחת פצע' (שמות 21:25), which the line just before said is needed.

phrases.english: and one forced by circumstances like one acting willingly!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a challenge that began just before this section, against the proof for paying צער with נזק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of 'פצע תחת פצע' to teach that צער is paid along with נזק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The phrase is already needed to make שוגג and אונס liable, so it may not be free to teach about צער.

steps.title: The longer wording teaches both lessons
steps.stepSummary: If the verse only meant to include שוגג and אונס, it could have said 'פצע בפצע'. Since it used the longer 'פצע תחת פצע', we learn both lessons from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let the verse write 'a wound for (ב) a wound.' Why does it say 'a wound in place of (תחת) a wound'? Learn two lessons from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The verse used extra, longer wording, so there is room for two lessons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The short form 'פצע בפצע' would have been enough to make שוגג and אונס liable. The word 'תחת', meaning 'in place of', is extra. So the verse teaches that the injurer is liable however it happened, and also that he pays צער along with נזק.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (if the verse meant only that)
Let the verse write (it could have said it differently)

steps.whatToRemember: One extra wording can teach two laws: liability for שוגג and אונס, and paying צער along with נזק.

phrases.english: If so, let the verse write:
'A wound for a wound';
Why does it say 'a wound in place of a wound'?
Learn two lessons from it.
phrases.notes: The two lessons: the injurer is liable even by accident or under force, and he pays for pain along with damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, נִכְתּוֹב קְרָא: פֶּצַע בְּפָצַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extra wording in the verse makes room for both lessons.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase only teaches that שוגג and אונס are liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: The longer wording 'תחת' teaches both that שוגג and אונס are liable and that צער is paid along with נזק.

steps.title: Medical costs are paid along with damage
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא in the name of רבא: from 'ורפא ירפא' we learn that one pays רפוי even when he also pays נזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said in the name of רבא: The verse says 'and he shall surely heal.' This teaches that one pays medical costs together with damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. רב פפא gives a source that the injurer pays medical costs on top of paying for the damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think the payment for נזק covers everything, so no separate payment for healing is needed. רב פפא learns from the doubled phrase 'ורפא ירפא' that medical costs are an additional payment, even where נזק is also paid.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And he shall surely heal', a doubled phrase about healing

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source that רפוי is a separate payment from נזק, one of the five payments an injurer makes.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said in the name of Rava:
The verse says: 'And he shall surely heal'
to give medical costs where there is damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא אָמַר, אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After proving צער is paid with נזק, the גמרא now brings a source that רפוי is paid with נזק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From 'ורפא ירפא', medical costs are paid together with damage.

steps.title: The verse is needed to permit doctors to heal
steps.stepSummary: The verse 'ורפא ירפא' is needed for the teaching of the school of רבי ישמעאל, that a doctor is permitted to heal.
steps.simpleTranslation: This verse is needed for what the school of רבי ישמעאל taught. The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: 'And he shall surely heal'. From here we learn that permission was given to a doctor to heal!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא. It says the verse is already used for a different lesson: permission for doctors to heal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'ורפא ירפא' teaches that a doctor is permitted to heal, then the phrase is already used up and may not be free to teach about paying medical costs.

keyTerms.meaning: This is needed for (a different lesson)
A teaching from the school of רבי ישמעאל

phrases.english: This is needed
for what the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught,
as the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
'And he shall surely heal' – from here
we learn that permission was given to a doctor to heal!

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי מִבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְכִדְתָנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's source in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's use of 'ורפא ירפא' to teach that רפוי is paid with נזק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse is already needed to teach that a doctor may heal, so it may not be free for another lesson.

steps.title: The verse could have said 'a doctor shall heal'
steps.stepSummary: If the verse only meant to permit doctors, it would have said 'ורופא ירפא'. Since it said 'ורפא', we learn that medical costs are paid along with damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let the verse write 'and a doctor (רופא) shall heal'! Learn from it that one pays medical costs together with damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It points out that the verse did not use the clearest wording for the doctor lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the doctor lesson, the natural wording would be 'ורופא ירפא', 'and a doctor shall heal'. The תורה wrote 'ורפא' instead. That change in wording is free to teach רב פפא's lesson about medical costs.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And a doctor shall heal', the wording the verse could have used

steps.confusionAlert: 'רפא' (healing) and 'רופא' (a doctor) look almost the same in Hebrew. The answer depends on that small difference in wording.

phrases.english: If so, let the verse write
'And a doctor shall heal'!
Learn from it
to give medical costs where there is damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, נִכְתּוֹב קְרָא וְרוֹפֵא יְרַפֵּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The verse did not use the most natural wording, which leaves room for another lesson.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'ורפא ירפא' is used up by the doctor lesson.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wording 'ורפא' instead of 'ורופא' teaches that רפוי is paid with נזק.

steps.title: The doubled healing language is still needed
steps.stepSummary: Even so, the verse still needs to repeat the language of healing for the lesson already mentioned, so the doubling proves nothing extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is still needed for what we said: the verse needed to repeat the language of healing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again. It says the repeated healing words are still needed for the earlier lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if 'רופא' was not used, the verse still had to say 'heal' twice to teach what was already explained. So the double language may not be extra, and it may not teach about medical costs.

phrases.english: But it is still needed for what we said,
for the verse to repeat in it the language of healing!
phrases.notes: The point is that saying 'heal' twice is still needed, so the doubling alone doesn't prove anything new.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge, after the answer in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 5 that the wording leaves room for the medical-costs lesson.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The repeated healing language is still needed for the earlier lesson, so nothing is left over.

steps.title: The mixed wording proves the medical-costs law
steps.stepSummary: If the verse only needed a repetition, it could have said 'רפא רפא' or 'ירפא ירפא'. Since it used the mixed form 'ורפא ירפא', we learn that medical costs are paid with damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let the verse say either 'רפא רפא' or 'ירפא ירפא'. Why does it say 'ורפא ירפא'? Learn from it that one pays medical costs together with damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its final answer. A plain repetition would have used the same word twice, but the verse switched forms, and that change teaches רב פפא's law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Repeating the same word twice would have been enough for the earlier lesson. The verse used two different forms instead, 'רפא' and then 'ירפא'. That change is extra, and it teaches that רפוי is paid along with נזק. רב פפא's teaching stands.

keyTerms.meaning: The same word repeated, one possible wording
The other word repeated, another possible wording

steps.whatToRemember: Every detail of 'ורפא ירפא' teaches something: the doubling and the change between word forms. In the end, רב פפא's law stands: medical costs are paid along with damage.

phrases.english: If so, let the verse say
either 'heal, heal'
or 'he shall heal, he shall heal',
why does it say 'and heal, he shall heal'?
Learn from it
to give medical costs where there is damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, לֵימָא קְרָא אוֹ רַפֹּא רַפֹּא אוֹ יְרַפֵּא יְרַפֵּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 6 and confirms רב פפא's teaching from step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The verse switches word forms, which is extra beyond a simple repetition.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The double language is fully used by the earlier lesson.
steps.terutzMaskana: The change from 'רפא' to 'ירפא' teaches that רפוי is paid with נזק.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Medical costs (רפוי) are paid in addition to damage (נזק), learned from the exact wording 'ורפא ירפא'.

steps.title: Inference that these payments can come without damage
steps.stepSummary: Saying that these payments are owed even when there is נזק implies that they can also be owed when there is no נזק at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: From this we can infer that these payments can be found even where there is no damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pulls a side point out of the teaching that these payments are owed even when there is also נזק. This line sets up the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying these payments are owed 'even' when there is נזק implies there are also cases where they come on their own, with no נזק. The גמרא now needs to show that such cases really exist.

keyTerms.meaning: by inference; from this we can learn
you find them; such cases exist
in a case where there is also damage (loss of a limb or of its use)

phrases.english: By inference, you can find them
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the payments for pain, medical costs, lost work and embarrassment.

phrases.english: not in a case of damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְלָל דְּמַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לְהוּ שֶׁלֹּא בִּמְקוֹם נֶזֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a side point from the conclusion that ריפוי is paid along with נזק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The extra payments can exist on their own, without נזק.

steps.title: Asking for examples without damage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a real case of each payment where there is no נזק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where there is no damage, how do you find these payments?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for real examples of each payment happening without any נזק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a clarifying question, not an attack. The inference from the previous step needs real cases to back it up.

phrases.english: Not in a case of damage
how do you find them?

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁלֹּא בִּמְקוֹם נֶזֶק הֵיכִי מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for cases that prove the inference.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Real cases of צער, ריפוי, שבת and בושת with no נזק.

steps.title: Examples for pain and medical costs
steps.stepSummary: צער alone: burning someone on the fingernail. ריפוי alone: giving a harsh drug that whitens the skin, so a second drug is needed to restore its color.
steps.simpleTranslation: Pain: as the משנה teaches, he burned him with a skewer or a nail, even on his fingernail, where no wound is made. Medical costs: something hurt him, and the other person brought him a harsh drug that turned his skin white. Now he must give him another drug to bring back the normal color of his skin.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its first two examples: a case of only צער, and a case of only ריפוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A burn on the fingernail hurts but leaves no wound and does no lasting harm, so it is pure צער. The whitened skin is not a loss of any body part or its use, so there is no נזק. He still needs treatment, so he must pay ריפוי.

keyTerms.meaning: as it is taught (here, in our משנה)

phrases.english: Pain: as it is taught:
phrases.notes: This refers to our משנה, which already gave this example.

phrases.english: Pain: he burned him with a skewer or with a nail,
and even on his fingernail,
a place where it makes no wound.
Medical costs: where something was hurting him,
and the other came and brought him a harsh drug,
and it turned his skin white;
so he must give him a drug
to bring back the color of his skin.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the question with the first two payments.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: צער alone: a burn on the fingernail. ריפוי alone: a harsh drug that whitened the skin.

steps.title: Examples for lost work and embarrassment
steps.stepSummary: שבת alone: locking someone in a room. בושת alone: spitting in someone's face.
steps.simpleTranslation: Lost work: he locked him in a room and kept him from working. Embarrassment: he spat in his face.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer with examples of שבת alone and בושת alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Locking someone up causes him to lose work time without hurting his body. Spitting in someone's face shames him without any injury. With these, all four payments have been shown to exist without נזק, which proves the inference from step 8.

keyTerms.meaning: kept him idle, stopped him from working

steps.whatToRemember: Each of the four extra payments (צער, ריפוי, שבת, בושת) can be owed by itself, even when there is no נזק at all.

phrases.english: Lost work: where he locked him in a room and kept him idle.
Embarrassment: where he spat in his face.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the list of examples.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שבת alone: locking someone in a room. בושת alone: spitting in his face.

steps.title: The משנה's rule for measuring lost work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: for שבת, the victim is valued as if he were a watchman of cucumbers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Lost work: we look at him as if he were a watchman of cucumbers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה and quotes its rule for measuring שבת, to begin talking about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Watching cucumbers is very easy, low-paying work, the kind of job an injured person can still do. So the משנה measures lost work time by this low wage.

keyTerms.meaning: we look at him; we assess him
a watchman of cucumbers, an easy and low-paying job

steps.confusionAlert: This is about the payment for time off work while healing, not the payment for the lost limb itself. The loss of the limb's value is already covered under נזק.

phrases.english: Lost work: we look at him
as if he were a watchman of cucumbers.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁבֶת – רוֹאִין אוֹתוֹ כְּאִילּוּ הוּא שׁוֹמֵר קִישּׁוּאִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new subject: the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שבת is valued at the wage of a watchman of cucumbers.

steps.title: A ברייתא repeats the rule
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches the same rule about the watchman of cucumbers, as an opening to its own discussion.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבנן taught: Lost work: we look at him as if he were a watchman of cucumbers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that repeats the משנה's rule. This sets up a question that the ברייתא itself is about to ask.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא adds nothing new yet. It repeats the rule so that it can go on to question how fair it is.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Lost work: we look at him
as if he were a watchman of cucumbers.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן שֶׁבֶת רוֹאִין אוֹתוֹ כְּאִילּוּ הוּא שׁוֹמֵר קִישּׁוּאִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that repeats the משנה's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Same rule: שבת is valued at the wage of a watchman of cucumbers.

steps.title: Is the cucumber-watchman rule unfair?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks: isn't this unfair to the victim? Once he heals, he will earn more by carrying water or working as a messenger.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say: justice has been harmed! Because when this man heals, he won't earn a cucumber watchman's wage. He'll carry buckets of water and earn more, or he'll go on errands as a messenger and earn more!
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises a fairness problem with paying only a cucumber watchman's wage, and the גמרא spells out why it seems unfair. The answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is that the low wage does not match what this man will really earn once he heals. Once healthy, he would do better-paying work, so paying him the lowest wage seems to shortchange him.

keyTerms.meaning: justice has been harmed; the result is unfair
draws or carries buckets of water

phrases.english: And if you say: justice has been harmed!
Because when this man heals,

phrases.aramaic: לָאו אַגְרָא דְּשׁוֹמֵר קִישּׁוּאִין הוּא שָׁקֵיל,
phrases.english: he won't be earning a cucumber watchman's wage,
rather he'll carry water buckets and earn a wage;

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי אָזֵיל בִּשְׁלִיח[וּתָא] וְשָׁקֵיל אַגְרָא!
phrases.english: or he'll go on errands as a messenger and earn a wage!
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are the corrected wording, making the word mean 'as a messenger.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the fairness of the rule just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that שבת is valued at a cucumber watchman's wage.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Once healed, the victim would earn higher wages doing harder work, so paying only the lowest wage seems to shortchange him.

steps.title: The payment is fair because the limb was already paid for
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers its question: justice is not harmed, because the injurer already paid the value of the hand or leg.
steps.simpleTranslation: The standard of justice was not damaged, because he already gave him the value of his hand and the value of his leg.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the question from Step 14. Paying שבת at the low cucumber-watchman rate is not unfair to the victim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 worried that the victim, once healed, could have earned more as a water carrier or messenger. The answer is that the money for the lost limb (נזק) already covered the better jobs he lost forever. So שבת only needs to cover the job he can still do, and that job is watching cucumbers.

keyTerms.meaning: The standard of justice; strict fairness
The value of his hand (the payment for the lost limb)

steps.whatToRemember: נזק pays for the permanent loss of ability. שבת pays only for the time off from the work he can still do.

phrases.english: The standard of justice was not damaged,
because he already gave him
the value of his hand and the value of his leg.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the fairness question raised in Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing: the loss the question pointed to was already paid under a different payment (נזק).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Measuring שבת as a cucumber watchman cheats the victim out of his higher future earnings.
steps.terutzMaskana: Those higher earnings were already paid for in the value of the limb, so nothing is lost.

steps.title: רבא: a lost hand and a broken leg
steps.stepSummary: רבא: for a cut-off hand, pay its value, and measure שבת as a cucumber watchman. For a broken leg, pay its value, and measure שבת as a doorway watchman.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If he cut off his hand, he gives him the value of his hand, and for loss of work we view him as a cucumber watchman. If he broke his leg, he gives him the value of his leg, and for loss of work we view him as a watchman at the doorway.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא applies the rule we just learned to specific injuries. He matches each injury to the easiest job the victim can still do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone without a hand can still walk around a field, so he can guard cucumbers. Someone with a broken leg cannot walk around, so he can only sit and guard a doorway. The job used to measure שבת changes depending on what the victim can still physically do.

keyTerms.meaning: Payment for loss of work time
We view him as if; we measure him as
A watchman at the doorway (an even easier job)

phrases.english: Rava said:
If he cut off his hand,
he gives him the value of his hand,
and for loss of work, we view him
as if he were a watchman of cucumbers.
If he broke his leg,
he gives him the value of his leg,
and for loss of work, we view him
as if he were a watchman at the doorway.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the principle settled in Step 15 and applies it to different injuries.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Lost hand: pay for the hand, with שבת at the cucumber-watchman rate. Broken leg: pay for the leg, with שבת at the doorway-watchman rate.

steps.title: רבא: blinding an eye and making someone deaf
steps.stepSummary: For a blinded eye, pay its value, and measure שבת as someone turning a millstone. For deafness, pay the victim's entire value.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he blinded his eye, he gives him the value of his eye, and for loss of work we view him as if he turns a millstone. If he made him deaf, he gives him his entire value.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא continues his list with two more injuries. Deafness gets a special, much bigger payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A blind person can still turn a millstone, so that job measures his שבת. For deafness, the injurer pays the victim's whole value. The victim is treated as unable to do any job at all, so there is no easier job left to measure him by.

keyTerms.meaning: His entire value (as if he were sold as a whole)

steps.confusionAlert: Deafness is not a limb payment plus שבת like the other cases. The injurer pays the person's whole value.

phrases.english: If he blinded his eye,
he gives him the value of his eye,
and for loss of work, we view him
as if he makes him grind with a millstone.
If he made him deaf,
he gives him his entire value.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's list from Step 16 and ends with the exceptional case of deafness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blinded eye: pay for the eye, with שבת at the millstone-turner rate. Deafness: pay the person's entire value.
steps.whyThisMatters: The full payment for deafness sets up רבא's question in the next step.

steps.title: רבא asks: several unassessed injuries, then deafness
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks: if hand, leg and eye were injured and none was assessed, and then the victim was made deaf, is there one assessment or a separate one for each injury?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: If he cut off his hand and they did not assess him, broke his leg and they did not assess him, blinded his eye and they did not assess him, and in the end made him deaf, what is the law? Do we say that since they did not assess him, one assessment is enough, and he gives him his entire value all at once? Or perhaps we assess each injury one by one and give him payment for each.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא raises a question (בעיא) that grows out of the list he just gave. The second side of the question runs straight into the next step, where רבא explains which payments are really at stake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since deafness alone means paying the whole value, maybe all the earlier unassessed injuries get swallowed into one big assessment. Or maybe each injury is a separate damage that gets its own assessment, which could make the total larger. The question is whether the lack of assessment joins the injuries together.

keyTerms.meaning: Asks a question that is not yet answered (a בעיא)

phrases.english: Rava asked:
If he cut off his hand and they did not assess him,
broke his leg and they did not assess him,
blinded his eye and they did not assess him,
and in the end made him deaf, what is the law?
Do we say:
since they did not assess him,
one assessment is enough for him,

phrases.aramaic: וְיָהֵיב לֵיהּ דְּמֵי כוּלֵּיהּ בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי?
phrases.english: and he gives him his entire value all at once?
Or perhaps,
we assess each one separately
and we give him (payment for each)

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the injuries from רבא's list (Steps 16 and 17) to build a new case that mixes them together.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: When several injuries were never assessed and the victim was then made deaf, is there one combined assessment (his entire value) or a separate assessment and payment for each injury?

steps.title: What is really at stake: pain and humiliation for each injury
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains the practical difference in his question. נזק, ריפוי and שבת are covered by the full-value payment for deafness. The open question is whether צער and בושת are paid separately for each injury.
steps.simpleTranslation: The practical difference is whether he must pay pain and humiliation for each injury. Granted, he does not pay damage, medical costs and lost work for each one. Since he pays the victim's full value, it is as if he killed him, and full value is paid. But must he still pay pain and humiliation for each one, since the victim did suffer pain and humiliation each time?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains exactly which payments his question from step 18 is about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Paying the full value for deafness is treated like paying for a whole person, so separate נזק, ריפוי and שבת for the hand, leg and eye are swallowed up. צער and בושת are different, because the victim really did feel pain and shame at each injury. So the question narrows to those two payments only.

keyTerms.meaning: Pain and humiliation, two of the five payments
Granted, even if we agree that
It is like one who killed him

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not asking whether to pay all five payments for each injury. He agrees that נזק, ריפוי and שבת are covered by the full value. Only צער and בושת are in doubt.

phrases.english: The practical difference is whether he must give him
pain and humiliation for each and every one;
granted that damage, medical costs and loss of work

phrases.aramaic: דְּכֹל חֲדָא וַחֲדָא לָא יָהֲבִינַן לֵיהּ –
phrases.english: for each and every one we do not give him

phrases.aramaic: דְּכֵיוָן דְּקָא יָהֵיב לֵיהּ דְּמֵי כוּלֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: because since he is giving him his entire value,
phrases.notes: The full value is owed because of the deafness, as in step 17.

phrases.english: he is like someone who killed him,
and he is giving him his entire value;

phrases.aramaic: צַעַר וּבוֹשֶׁת מִיהַת דְּכֹל חֲדָא וַחֲדָא יָהֵיב,
phrases.english: but pain and humiliation, at least, does he give for each and every one,
since he did have pain and humiliation?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains what practical result hangs on רבא's question in step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether צער and בושת are paid separately for each injury when the victim's full value is paid for deafness.

steps.title: What if each injury was already assessed?
steps.stepSummary: Suppose the answer is that without assessments, only the full value is paid. What if the court did assess each injury, but the injurer had not paid yet before making the victim deaf?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that because they did not assess him, he pays the full value all together, what if they did assess him? Do we say that because they assessed him, he must pay each injury separately? Or perhaps, because he had not yet paid, he just gives the full value?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא builds a second question on top of the first one, changing the case so that the court had already assessed each injury.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case, there were no assessments, so maybe everything merges into one full-value payment. Here each injury was already assessed, which might make each one a fixed debt of its own. Or maybe it still merges, because nothing was actually paid yet.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (introduces a follow-up question built on one possible answer)

phrases.english: And if you say:
since they did not assess him,

phrases.aramaic: קָא יָהֵיב לֵיהּ דְּמֵי כּוּלֵּיהּ בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי;
phrases.english: he gives him his entire value all together;
if they did assess him, what is the law?
Do we say: since they assessed him,
he must give him each one separately;
or perhaps, since he had not paid,
he gives him his entire value?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Assumes one answer to the first question and asks a further question with a changed case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an assessment that was made, but not paid, makes each injury a separate payment, or whether it still merges into the full value.

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends רבא's question with תיקו: it stands without an answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes רבא's questions without deciding them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source is found to settle either of רבא's questions. Both stay open: the case where the injuries were never assessed (are צער and בושת paid for each one?) and the case where they were assessed but not yet paid.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question is left unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: When injuries were never assessed and the victim ends up deaf, רבא grants that נזק, ריפוי and שבת merge into the full value. Two questions stay as תיקו: whether צער and בושת are paid for each injury, and whether injuries that were already assessed are paid separately.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends רבא's questions from steps 18–20 without a resolution.

steps.title: רבה asks about a loss of work that lowers value
steps.stepSummary: רבה asks a new question: what is the law when an injury causes a loss of work that lowers the victim's value?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה asked: lost work that lowers his value, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. רבה asks about an injury that makes the victim worth less, but only for a while.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This opens a new topic, separate from the deafness case. The גמרא will explain the exact case in the next step.

phrases.english: רבה asked:
loss of work that lowers his value, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new question after the previous one ended in תיקו.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether payment is owed for a temporary drop in the victim's value.

steps.title: The case: a weakened hand that will heal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defines the case: he hit the victim's hand and it shriveled, but it will return to health. Does he pay nothing, since it will heal, or does he pay because right now the victim is worth less?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? For example, he hit him on his hand and the hand shriveled, but it will eventually heal. What is the law? Since it will heal, does he pay nothing at all? Or perhaps, right now he has lowered his value?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the exact case of רבה's question and lays out both sides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One side looks at the end: the hand will be fine, so there is no lasting damage to pay for. The other side looks at the present: right now the victim would sell for less, so a loss did happen.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How does it look?

phrases.english: What is the case?
For example, he hit him on his hand
and his hand shriveled, but it will eventually heal;
What is the law? Since it will eventually heal,
he does not give him anything at all;
phrases.notes: This is talking about payment for the damage itself, the drop in value.

phrases.english: or perhaps, right now at least he has lowered his value?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the case of רבה's question and lays out both sides.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a temporary drop in value require payment, or does the fact that it will heal cancel it?

steps.title: A proof begins from a משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts quoting a משנה about someone who hits his parents without a bruise, or injures someone on יום הכפורים. The proof continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: One who hits his father or mother and did not make a bruise on them, and one who injures his fellow on יום הכפורים...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins bringing a source to answer רבה's question. This is only the start of the quote; the proof comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These cases are chosen because they are not punished by death in court, so money can still be owed. The rest of the משנה will show what is paid, and that may settle רבה's question.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
one who hits his father or his mother
and did not make a bruise on them,
and one who injures his fellow on יום הכפורים

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a proof for רבה's question.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's question about a temporary drop in value.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A משנה about hitting parents without a bruise and injuring on יום הכפורים (continues in the next section).
